old_strategy: (i) contraposes the Blaschke-condition theorem. (ii) uses the identity $1-|b_a(z)|^2=\frac{(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{|1-\overline az|^2}$ and $|1-\overline{a_n}z|\to|1-z|>0$ for fixed $z$, giving divergence of $\sum(1-|b_{a_n}(z)|)$; the partial products are decreasing in modulus, and pointwise convergence of a decreasing sequence of continuous functions to the continuous limit $0$ on a compact set is uniform (Dini). (iii) is the published zero-divisor theorem on plane domains applied to the discrete set $\{1-1/n\}\subset\mathbb D$.
new_strategy: For a_n=1-1/n (n>=2), 1-|a_n|=1/n gives harmonic divergence and rules out every nonzero H^p realization by the Blaschke necessary condition. On a nonempty compact K in the disc with rho=max_K|z|<1, the factor modulus identity yields 1-|b_{a_n}(z)| >= (1-rho^2)/(8n), uniformly on K. Thus the normal-convergence deviation sum diverges, while |B_N(z)| <= exp[-(1-rho^2)/8 sum_{n=2}^N 1/n] (and any prescribed factor zero makes the product zero) proves locally uniform convergence of the partial products to zero. For the holomorphic witness, a_n in K implies n<=1/(1-rho), so the prescribed support is compactly finite; apply the corrected plane-domain zero-divisor theorem with multiplicity one to obtain a nonzero holomorphic function with exactly these simple zeros, which lies in no H^p.
